'''''Myoporum acuminatum''''', commonly known as '''waterbush''', '''pointed boobialla''' or '''mangrove boobialla''',<ref name=Floyd2008>{{cite book |url=http://rainforestpublishing.com.au/shop/rainforest-trees-of-south-eastern-australia/ |title=Rainforest Trees of Mainland South-eastern Australia |first=A. G. |last=Floyd |author-link=Alexander Floyd |publisher=Terania Rainforest Publishing |location=[[Lismore, New South Wales]] |year=2008 |edition=2nd, Revised |isbn= 978-0-958943-67-3 |page=412 |access-date=2010-09-14}}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] in the figwort [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Scrophulariaceae]] and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern [[Australia]]. It grows in [[rainforest]] or wet [[eucalyptus]] forest near the coast and in the Coastal Ranges, and is occasionally associated with [[mangrove]]s. Occasionally it is found in the drier rainforests. It grows naturally as far south as [[Mimosa Rocks National Park]] in far south eastern [[New South Wales]], and north to [[Fraser Island]] in Southern [[Queensland]].<ref name="ReferenceA">Chinnock, R.J. 2007 "Eremophila and Allied Genera: A Monograph of the Plant Family Myoporaceae". The Botanic Gardens and State Herbarium of South Australia. Adelaide.</ref>

== Description ==
''Myoporum acuminatum'' grows as a hairless shrub or small tree, up to 13 metres (40 ft) tall and a trunk diameter of 50 cm (20 in). In larger plants the trunk may be irregular in shape with flanges. Bark is greyish brown and somewhat wrinkled in larger trees. Small branches are green and fairly thick, though smooth.<ref name=Floyd2008/>

''M. acuminatum'' has been considered by some authors to encompass ''[[Myoporum montanum]]''.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> The two species are closely  and related and ''M. montanum'' has an overlapping range. The common name Waterbush is originally derived from ''M. montanum'', which grows throughout arid central Australia as well as coastal regions, and whose presence is thought to be indicative of groundwater.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.australianseed.com/product_info.php/pName/myoporum-montanum-western-boobialla/osCsid=04c7edf62fd347fc79cc67dbb35284fc |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130117102448/http://www.australianseed.com/product_info.php/pName/myoporum-montanum-western-boobialla/osCsid=04c7edf62fd347fc79cc67dbb35284fc |url-status=dead |archive-date=2013-01-17 |title=myoporum montanum western boobialla |website=www.australianseed.com}}</ref>

The species are difficult to distinguish, being closely related with an overlapping range. ''M. montanum'' has smaller, narrower leaves, the flower [[sepal]]s of ''M. montanum'' lack the translucent margins of ''M. acuminatum'' and the fruit of ''M. montanum'' is pink or light purple compared with the dark purple or blue fruit of ''M. acuminatum''.

=== Leaves ===
Leaves are 5 to 14 cm long and 7 to 28 mm wide<ref name=plantnet>{{cite web |title=''Myoporum acuminatum''|work= PlantNET - NSW Flora Online|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Myoporum~acuminatum|accessdate=2010-09-14}}</ref> with a fine point, though rarely seen with a rounded end. The base of the leaf becomes thin near the leaf stem, which measures 6 to 20 mm long. Leaf edges may be finely toothed, or smooth. Leaves lack [[stipule]]s. Oil dots of varying sizes may be seen under a magnifying lens, of a distance apart of 3 to 5 diameters. Only the midrib is easily seen, other lateral or net veins are obscure.<ref name=Floyd2008/>

=== Flowers and fruit ===
Flowers appear from May to August, though later in the southern parts of its range. Flowers feature five white petals, with four rows of purple spots and a sweet scent. They grow in clusters from the leaf [[axil]]s.<ref name=Floyd2008/>

The fruit is a roughened, wrinkled [[drupe]]. Globular in shape, 5 mm in diameter, dark blue or dark purple in colour. Remnants of the flower [[style (botany)|style]] point out of the fruit, 3 to 4 mm long and ''hooked''. Inside are two to four seeds, maturing from October to February.<ref name=Floyd2008/><ref name="ReferenceA"/>

==Taxonomy==
The plant first appeared in scientific literature in ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae]]'' in 1810, authored by [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]].<ref>{{APNI | name = ''Myoporum acuminatum'' R.Br. | id = 34041}}</ref><ref name=Brown>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Robert|title=Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae|date=1810|location=London|page=515|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/21871#page/383/mode/1up|accessdate=11 March 2018}}</ref> The genus name ''Myoporum'' refers to the [[Ancient Greek]] roots ''myein'' meaning "to shut" or "to close" and ''πόρος (poros)'' meaning "opening" or "pore"<ref name=Quattrocchi>{{cite book|last1=Quattrocchi|first1=Umberto|title=CRC world dictionary of plant names : common names, scientific names, eponyms, synonyms, and etymology (Volume III; M-Q)|date=1999|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton, FL|isbn=0849326737|page=1752|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kaN-hLL-3qEC&q=Greek+myo+myein&pg=PA1752|accessdate=31 August 2015}}</ref> referring to the closed glands which appear as transparent spots on the leaves, flowers and fruits.<ref name=Chinnock(1)>{{cite book|last1=Chinnock|first1=R.J.|title=Eremophila and allied genera : a monograph of the plant family Myoporaceae|date=2007|publisher=Rosenberg|location=Dural, NSW|isbn=9781877058165|page=95|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5iZlQOKoEjoC&q=betcheanum&pg=PA128|accessdate=31 August 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''acuminatum'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "tapering to a prolonged point".<ref name="Sharr">{{cite book |author=Francis Aubie Sharr |author-link=Francis Aubie Sharr |title=Western Australian Plant Names and their Meanings |date=2019 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya, Western Australia |isbn=9780958034180 |page=127}}</ref><ref name="ReferenceA" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Myoporum acuminatum'' grows in [[rainforest]] or [[eucalyptus]] forest of eastern Australia, from Queensland to the far south coast of New South Wales.<ref name=plantnet/>

==Use in horticulture==
Waterbush is a hardy plant in cultivation and can tolerate salt spray. It prefers well drained soil in full sun and is most easily propagated from cuttings.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0002165759|page=271|edition=2nd}}</ref>
